title: US Strikes Container Ship Off Pakistan Coast for Defying Iran Blockade
excerpt: The Panama-flagged Vela Nova, which recently called at Mumbai, becomes the 12th vessel disabled by U.S. forces since the blockade began in April.
body:
• U.S. Central Command fired two Hellfire missiles at the Panama-flagged container ship Vela Nova in the Gulf of Oman, disabling its steering gear after the vessel ignored repeated warnings about violating the naval blockade on Iranian ports.
  • The strike — approximately 71 nautical miles off Pakistan's coast — marks the 12th vessel disabled by U.S. forces since the blockade was announced in April and the third since it was reimposed on July 14.
  • The Vela Nova had recently called at Mumbai, India, and Port Klang, Malaysia, both locations where Iran-linked ships have been spotted.
  • In a separate incident, four crew members including three Pakistanis were killed in a Houthi attack on a cargo ship in the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

U.S. Central Command fired two Hellfire missiles at a Panama-flagged container ship in the Gulf of Oman on Tuesday, disabling the vessel after it ignored repeated warnings to stop violating the naval blockade on Iranian ports, according to Reuters.

The ship, identified as the Vela Nova, had its steering gear knocked out roughly 71 nautical miles (131 km) off Pakistan's coast, according to UK maritime risk management group Vanguard. It is the 12th vessel disabled by U.S. forces since the blockade was announced in April, and the third since the blockade was reimposed on July 14.

Mumbai Port Call Draws Scrutiny

The Vela Nova recently made port calls in Mumbai, India, and Port Klang, Malaysia — both locations where Iran-linked ships have also been spotted, according to Charlie Brown, senior advisor at United Against Nuclear Iran, a U.S. advocacy group that monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking.

https://x.com/DailyNewsEgypt/status/2087313454256345475

"The reported U.S. disabling and stopping of the Panama-flagged Vela Nova near the blockade line in the Gulf of Oman, after its recent Mumbai port call alongside these vessels, underscores the heightened scrutiny now being applied to Iran-related shipping."

— Charlie Brown, Senior Advisor, United Against Nuclear Iran

The UK Maritime Trade Operations confirmed the incident, initially describing the vessel as a tanker before correcting it to a container ship. Maritime security sources confirmed a missile was involved in the strike.

Deadly Houthi Attack Kills Three Pakistanis

In a separate incident the same day, four crew members were killed when Iran-backed Houthis attacked the cargo ship Tihamah in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, Yemen's transport ministry said. Three of the dead were Pakistani nationals, Pakistan's foreign minister confirmed. One Indonesian crew member was also killed.

Two rescuers from the National Resistance Forces, an anti-Houthi military group, were also killed when the Houthis struck again after rescue crews arrived, the Yemeni Coast Guard said. Ten people were injured in the attacks, including seven crew members and three coast guard and NRF personnel.

The fatalities would mark the first deaths from a Houthi strike on shipping since the Iran war began on February 28. The Houthis declared a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea on July 20, saying it was a response to what they described as a Saudi siege. Riyadh denies that Yemen is under siege.

Shipping Lanes Under Siege

Traffic through the region's key chokepoints has cratered. An average of 32 ships per day passed through the Bab el-Mandeb strait last week — down from 50 before the blockade, according to Kpler data. Shipping through the strait and Red Sea has fallen by more than 50% overall since the earlier wave of Houthi attacks.

The Strait of Hormuz has been hit even harder, with just six ships passing through on Monday, compared with pre-war levels of 130 to 140 vessels per day, according to Reuters data.

What to Watch

The simultaneous disruptions to two of the world's most critical shipping corridors continue to reshape global maritime commerce. For South Asian nations — India imports more than 80% of its oil, much of it transiting these waterways — the consequences are immediate. Indian state refiner Bharat Petroleum recently reported that discounts on Russian crude delivered to India have evaporated amid the Middle East turmoil, squeezing margins for refiners that sell fuel at subsidized domestic rates.

With the U.S. blockade enforcement intensifying and Houthi attacks expanding to target vessels linked to Saudi Arabia, the risks facing commercial shipping in the region show no signs of easing.
